newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - US May foreign trade gap $10.23 bln.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - US May foreign trade gap $10.23 bln.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department said the May international trade deficit widened to $10.23 billion against a revised $8.75 billion in April.
Economists in a Reuters survey had expected a $9.18 billion deficit in the May foreign trade report.

ALAN RUSKIN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "I don't think the dollar is going to take off" on the 25-percent narrowing of the U.S.-Japan trade gap. Ruskin said Federal Reserve or Bank of Japan intervention levels are probably above 120 yen.
Ruskin was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.
ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "It's surprising that exports didn't do better, because there was such a jump in the aircraft.
"The data itself, taken at surface, would suggest they would not boost (second-quarter) growth. (Economists) are probably going to have a softer GDP estimate ... in the second quarter," she added.

CARL WEINBERG, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HIGH FREQUENCY ECONOMICS: "It's wider than expected ... we were looking for a widening, but basically it looks as if the U.S. economy is hot and we're paying the price on the trade figures.
"I would expect this (overall report) to be weak for the dollar; I would expect this ... to take some of the steam off the (dollar versus the) deutschemark," Weinberg concluded.

KEVIN LOGAN, SENIOR MARKET ECONOMIST, DRESDNER KLEINWORT BENSON NORTH AMERICA LLC: "Numbers are neutral as far as financial markets are concerned. The six-month average is $9.5 billion, so we're close enough that there won't be much consequence.
"The trade balance deteriorated last year, but now it seems to have stablized. Gradually, the trade balance will worsen this year."

JAMES PADINHA, ECONOMIST, BRIEFING.COM: "The numbers were exactly what we were expecting ... The point here in terms of the bigger picture is that we're talking about a trade subtraction in terms of second quarter growth. We haven't had the time to type every single number yet, but (the impact) looks like about $10.0 billion, or six tenths of one percent.
Padinha said he was maintaining his forecast for second quarter GDP growth at 2.0 percent. He believes the U.S. economy will expand by 4.0 percent in the third quarter.
On the narrowing trade gap between the U.S. and Japan he said, "This helps, but we don't think it's going to be a big deal (for the foreign exchange market)."

PETER D'ANTONIO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, CITICORP GLOBAL FINANCE: "The deficit was a little wider than expected. The surprise is that imports didn't fall. It probably doesn't mean much in the context of GDP. All of the widening occurred in the capital goods area and we don't use expenditure numbers to calculate capital goods in the GDP. We estimate that GDP grew 1.2 percent in the second quarter.

"We've seen this huge run-up in exports and that coincided with a big run-up in shipments. And we had seen shipments fall off in May, so it's not too surprising that exports came off a bit. But they still seem to be on the strong side."
